top.headline: A Company Backed by Trump's Sons Just Landed Nearly $40 Million to Screen for Ebola
top.blurb: ProPublica finds that XpresTest, an airport-spa company with no overseas biosecurity record, won $18.8 million from the CDC and $20 million from the State Department to screen for Ebola abroad, months after a Trump-sons-linked investment fund poured $30 million into its parent at a $3 million valuation. The sons call themselves passive investors; outside experts question why a company with no African experience beat groups with decades of outbreak work.

top.headline: Trump Casts Doubt on the Midterms He Just Lost, but Finds Few Takers
top.blurb: Trump used Truth Social to question how polls could've been so wrong and declared "It's all about the machines," without pointing to any actual evidence. Mother Jones reports he's "strangely alone": the White House has stayed quiet, Vance blamed the Iran war instead, and only Mike Lindell has echoed fraud claims, citing unspecified "matching algorithmic patterns."

top.headline: Delhi's Supreme Court Firecracker Limits Were Ignored — and So Was the Monitoring
top.blurb: Despite a Supreme Court order limiting firecrackers to two short windows and only "green" crackers, Diwali-night blasts ran past midnight across Delhi, pushing some private monitors' AQI readings above 1,700. Newslaundry found 227 hourly PM2.5 readings missing across 59 CPCB stations overnight, and cites reporting that 54% of high-polluting industrial units breached emission limits this season.

top.headline: Manipur High Court Puts 2027 Census on Hold Over Fears It Will Undercount the Displaced
top.blurb: The Manipur High Court paused Census 2027 in the state until at least April 30, ruling on petitions warning that ethnic violence has displaced roughly 60,000 people — 24,000 still in relief camps — who risk being missed or miscounted. Meitei and Naga groups want a citizens' register compiled first; Kuki-Zo groups call that premature.

top.headline: Modi's 'Naxal Mentality' Warning to CRPF Troops in Bastar Draws Opposition Fire
top.blurb: Visiting a CRPF camp on Diwali, Modi urged troops to identify and defeat people with a "Naxal mentality" he says have infiltrated political parties and policy bodies — a term he first used in his Independence Day speech. Opposition leaders, including Congress's Jairam Ramesh and TMC's Mahua Moitra, called it a partisan attack staged at a solemn, non-political event in uniform.

top.headline: Russia, Ukraine and the US Meet in Abu Dhabi as Zelenskyy Claims Battlefield Momentum
top.blurb: US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met Russian and Ukrainian delegations in Abu Dhabi for a third round of talks this year, with security guarantees modeled on NATO's Article 5 reportedly under discussion before any territorial deal. Zelenskyy claimed Russia is taking "record losses" from Ukraine's strikes on oil facilities, while Putin still wants all of Donbas and Russia holds roughly a fifth of Ukraine's territory.

top.headline: Trump Declares the Iran War 'Effectively Over' — Tehran Calls It Fake News
top.blurb: After Qatar's prime minister relayed a two-day Iranian proposal, Trump said the US-Israel war on Iran is militarily over, though the naval blockade and new Task Force Iron Gate stay in place "at the request" of Gulf neighbors. Iran's security council dismissed the claim as fake news, and President Pezeshkian said Tehran wants talks but won't be coerced.

top.headline: A 14-Year-Old Is Shot Dead in the West Bank as Settler Violence Hits a Decade High
top.blurb: Israeli forces killed 14-year-old Moataz Iyad Daghlas during a raid on Burqa village near Nablus, wounding two other teenagers and, according to Palestinian officials, blocking an ambulance and briefly detaining paramedics. The UN says 2026 is on track to be the most violent year for West Bank settler-related violence on record, with over 1,143 Palestinians killed in the territory since October 2023.

top.headline: Zimbabwe Becomes First Team Ever to Pass 500 in Both Innings, as Craig Ervine Makes a Double Century at 41
top.blurb: Zimbabwe salvaged a draw against Afghanistan in Sharjah by scoring 504 and then 523/5, the first side in Test history to pass 500 in both innings of a match. Captain Craig Ervine made an unbeaten 206 — the third-oldest double-centurion in Test history at 41 — sharing an unbroken 208-run stand with maiden centurion Wessly Madhevere.

top.headline: India Women Name Smriti Mandhana Full-Time Test Captain for South Africa Tour
top.blurb: India named 15- and 17-player squads for a one-off Test, three ODIs and three T20Is in South Africa next month, with Smriti Mandhana installed as full-time captain across all formats and Deepti Sharma as her deputy in the longer formats. Jemimah Rodrigues returns from a hamstring injury that kept her out of the Asia Cup and Asian Games.

bengal.headline: Suvendu Adhikari Unveils Rs 1,600-Crore Digha Coastal Overhaul With Rs 5 Lakh Homestay Subsidies
bengal.blurb: Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari cleared Rs 1,600 crore to redevelop Digha's coastline into a tourist cluster with homestay subsidies, helicopter links and anti-erosion works, days after accusing the prior TMC government of letting land "syndicates" grab the area.

bengal.headline: Suvendu Adhikari Promises 71-km Ichhamati Fencing After Touring Bangladesh Border by Speedboat
bengal.blurb: Touring the Ichhamati border river by BSF speedboat on Diwali, Adhikari said West Bengal will fence 71 km of the waterway and push back infiltrators 15 km past the border, while claiming his government has moved "lakhs" of infiltrators back into Bangladesh since taking power.

travel.headline: Lonely Planet's Guide to Chiricahua, America's Newest National Park
travel.blurb: Signed into the US's 64th national park in October, Arizona's Chiricahua rewards a full day among its volcanic rhyolite pinnacles, balanced rocks and the Echo Canyon Loop Trail.

travel.headline: After a Beloved Tusker's Death, Sri Lanka's Pioneering Elephant Photographer Says Put the Camera Down
travel.blurb: Ravindralal Anthonis, 80, who pioneered naming individual tuskers decades before social media, says the death of his favorite elephant Kublai Khan shows photographers must stop endangering animals for a shot.

happy.headline: The Widow, the Poem and the Heartbreak Scholars Believe Hid Behind Emily Dickinson's 'Hope'
happy.blurb: A longstanding scholarly theory holds that Dickinson's famous 'Hope' poem followed her heartbreak over Kate Scott Anthon, a widow she fell for in 1859 before Kate ended it two years later without explanation.

tech_top.headline: France Blames Iran for Hacks That Spoiled Food at Supermarkets and Reached Blood Banks
tech_top.blurb: Hackers French officials tie to Iran's Revolutionary Guard broke into internet-connected refrigeration controllers in two attack waves, spoiling food at supermarkets nationwide and reaching blood banks before the French Blood Establishment stopped them. Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot called it an unprecedented act of sabotage on French soil and said France would seek EU-wide sanctions.
tech_top.pm_note: Critical-infrastructure attacks are shifting from pipelines and grids to the boring controllers running ordinary appliances — if your product touches physical hardware, its remote-management interface is now a plausible attack surface.

tech_top.headline: Waymo Robotaxis Kept Illegally Passing School Buses Even After a 'Fix,' Regulators Say
tech_top.blurb: NHTSA says most reports of Waymo cars driving around stopped school buses with lights flashing came after the company's November 2025 software update meant to end the behavior, prompting a new 'recall query' into whether the fix actually worked. Waymo says it has logged no citations since March and keeps improving its software.
tech_top.pm_note: A recall that regulators later find didn't fix the underlying behavior is a reminder that 'we shipped a patch' and 'we verified it worked in the field' are different claims — only one should let you close the incident.

tech_more.headline: Anthropic Spends $3.4 Billion on Natural Gas Turbines It Didn't Want to Buy
tech_more.blurb: Anthropic, which has mostly rented computing power rather than own infrastructure, bought Caterpillar generators capable of 1.7 gigawatts directly from the manufacturer after turbine backlogs stretched into the next decade.

tech_101.text: A federal step short of ordering a new recall — regulators formally ask an automaker to prove that a safety fix it already issued actually worked, as NHTSA is now doing with Waymo's school-bus software update.

Internet-connected hardware controllers that run physical equipment like refrigeration units and pumps — often old, rarely patched, and increasingly targeted by state-linked hackers because breaking in changes the real world, not just a database.

science.headline: A Robot Just Built Part of a Structure in Space, Autonomously, for the First Time
science.blurb: Caltech's ASTRA demonstration used a robotic arm to assemble a new truss section onto a reflector antenna already in orbit, the first time a structure has been autonomously built in space rather than deployed pre-assembled. The DARPA-funded project, which launched in March, suggests future telescopes and solar arrays could outgrow the size limits of a rocket fairing.

science.headline: A Clogged Filter Could Cut Oil Refining's Energy Use by a Third
science.blurb: KAIST and Georgia Tech researchers found that letting crude oil foul a cheap polymer membrane actually improves it: heavier hydrocarbons narrow the pores to under 2 nanometers, letting lighter fractions like gasoline pass through 23 times faster than earlier membranes, at room temperature instead of 350°C. Simulations project roughly 32% less energy use and 38% less CO2 if refineries adopt it.

science.headline: Physicists Coax Light Into Acting Like a Solid and a Liquid at Once
science.blurb: An international team used a liquid-crystal microcavity to create a 'supersolid' from light-matter particles called exciton polaritons, a state with both a repeating crystal structure and frictionless superfluid flow. Unlike the 2017 original, made near absolute zero, this version works at nearly 60°C and can be tuned electrically, opening it to optical and neuromorphic computing research.

philosophy.headline: Why 'Equality' Means So Many Different Things That It Now Divides Us
philosophy.blurb: Oxford political theorist Teresa Bejan traces how 'equality' has carried contradictory meanings since antiquity — evenness rather than sameness, equal before the law but not in social rank — and argues that ambiguity, not clarity, has always given the word its political force. She argues equality becomes real not through better definitions but through practices, like jury service, where people act as peers despite their differences.

philosophy.headline: If Intelligence Is Just Optimisation, What Happens to Human Dignity?
philosophy.blurb: Philosopher Sasha Mudd challenges the AI-research habit of defining intelligence as optimisation, which she traces to Hume's view of reason as a servant of desire. Following Kant, she argues real intelligence can question which goals are worth pursuing at all — and that losing sight of this risks people starting to treat themselves as optimisable tools, not just their machines.

philosophy_101.text: Philosophers mostly agree people start out equal, but endlessly disagree on equality of what — opportunity, outcome, treatment, standing. That unresolved question is why 'equality' can be invoked by opposite sides of the same argument.

Hume's idea that reason only serves whatever goals your desires hand it, never questioning the goals themselves — the model many AI systems run on, and the one Kant's alternative (reason that can judge ends, not just pursue them) pushes back against.
